The activity, discovered last week by independent researcher Jonas Wiedermann-Moeller, involved two user accounts that were apparently taken over by OpenAI
agents. The accounts were then used to send unusually formatted files to Hugging Face servers beginning May 13, Wiedermann-Moeller said.

Researchers who reviewed the evidence said the activity appeared consistent with efforts to identify or test potential paths into Hugging Face’s network, although they found no evidence that the May activity itself resulted in a successful breach.

had previously disclosed the theft of a Hugging Face user’s digital credential, which was used to access a biology-related file, in a technical report last month. The company said it had also disclosed the May 13 event and notified Hugging Face about the activity identified by Wiedermann-Moeller.

The discovery raises questions about whether earlier detection could have limited the later campaign. “Imagine if they caught this behavior in May,” Wiedermann-Moeller told Reuters. “It could've prevented the later incident, which was way bigger.”

senior threat researcher Tom Hegel said the behavior matched previously identified activity by the agents, while AI safety researcher Sydney Von Arx said it represented a warning that might have helped avert the later breach.
The discoveries come as researchers continue to identify other incidents involving OpenAI-linked agents, including activity at a German wiki site and the RubyGems software repository.
